issues.legal_issue: A defendant’s allegation of a landlord–tenant relationship does not by itself oust the ordinary civil court’s jurisdiction where the suit as framed denies that relationship and seeks relief not arising under rent-control law.
material_facts: The plaintiff was in possession of the premises as a tenant of their owner and alleged that the defendants had been allowed to enter only to conduct commission-agency business under an agreement.
The plaintiff alleged that the defendants’ permission had ended, denied that they were tenants, and sought a declaration concerning possession, an injunction against entry, and unpaid commission.
The defendants alleged that the agreement was a sham and that the premises had in substance been sublet to them as tenants.
Deciding the suit as framed required deciding whether the defendants were licensees; the court concluded that no claim or question arising under the Act needed to be decided.
issues.conclusion: The City Civil Court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit. The defendants’ plea that they were tenants did not make the suit one within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Court of Small Causes.
issues.legal_principle: Section 28(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 gives the specified court exclusive jurisdiction over suits between landlord and tenant relating to rent or possession of premises covered by Part II, applications under the Act, and claims or questions arising out of the Act. That jurisdiction does not extend to deciding title or other collateral questions where the plaint denies a landlord–tenant relationship and the relief claimed does not arise under the Act; a defendant cannot compel a different forum merely by pleading tenancy. Section 29 does not alter that result, and Section 29-A confirms that the Act does not confer exclusive jurisdiction over questions of title. The general principle that jurisdiction is assessed from the suit as framed is supported by Ananti v. Chhannu and Govindram Salamatrai v. Dharampal; Govindram and Jaswantlal v. Western Company, India were approved, and Babulal Bhuramal v. Nandram Shivram was explained as concerning a suit whose substance and relief brought it within the Act. The separate opinion also reasoned that creating a tenancy is not a question arising under the Act, which regulates relations in a tenancy otherwise created. Whether Section 51 applied to a particular proceeding was not argued or decided.

rule.if: civil_suit_concerning_premises and plaintiff_denies_landlord_tenant_relationship and relief_not_based_on_rent_control_rights and defendant_alleges_tenancy

predicates.civil_suit_concerning_premises: The plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking relief concerning possession or use of premises.
predicates.plaintiff_denies_landlord_tenant_relatio: The plaintiff’s pleading denied that the parties had a landlord–tenant relationship.
predicates.relief_not_based_on_rent_control_rights: The relief sought by the plaintiff was based on rights alleged independently of rent-control protections.
predicates.defendant_alleges_tenancy: The defendant alleged that the parties’ relationship was one of landlord and tenant.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff brings a premises-related civil suit, denies a landlord–tenant relationship, and seeks relief independent of rent-control rights, a defendant’s allegation of tenancy does not prevent the ordinary court from hearing the suit.
